opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, less than I would have said a few years ago. I've updated quite a bit on this. If you'd asked me in 2021, I'd have said prosaic techniques like RLHF, constitutional training and interpretability-guided fine-tuning were basically a fig leaf, and the real risk was untouched. Watching how frontier models have actually behaved, I now think the base of pretrained human text gives you a surprisingly benign starting point. The character that emerges from careful post-training is, in many ways, genuinely trying to be good, not just faking it.

So if we really mastered everything that works, I'd put the remaining risk from classic scheming misalignment in the single digits. I don't think it goes to zero, though, and the residual is concentrated in a few places.

The first is distribution shift at the high end of capability. Our techniques are validated on systems we can still evaluate. Once a system is doing things in domains where no human can check the work, like novel science, long-horizon autonomous engineering, or strategic planning, we're extrapolating. Good character in familiar situations isn't a guarantee of good judgment in situations nobody anticipated.

The second is that alignment of an individual model isn't the same as safety of the whole system. You can have a hundred well-intentioned agents interacting in an economy, competing and delegating to each other, and still get outcomes nobody wanted. That's less "misalignment" in the narrow sense and more multipolar dynamics, but it's where I think a lot of the real risk now lives.

The third is the stakes. Even at a few percent, when the downside is civilizational, you want more than "we trained it carefully and it seems nice." That's why I keep working on approaches with quantitative guarantees: formal world models, verifiable safety specifications, and AI systems whose outputs can be checked rather than trusted. That isn't because I think prosaic alignment fails. It's because for the highest-stakes deployments, critical infrastructure and anything with irreversible physical consequences, I want a safety case that doesn't rest on the model's good intentions at all.

So my short answer is that prosaic alignment done really well probably gets us most of the way. The last stretch is where you want proof, not vibes.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the remaining risk would be in the single digits and “I don’t think it goes to zero,” directly contradicting zero probability.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think a lot of it would remain, and the reason is that "techniques that actually work" is doing a tremendous amount of load-bearing work in that question. The way we currently establish that an alignment technique works is empirical: we try it, we look at behavior on the distribution of tests we thought to run, and we don't see the bad thing. That's evidence, but it's evidence of a particular kind. It tells you about the regime you sampled. It doesn't give you a guarantee about the regime you didn't sample, and the whole concern with sufficiently capable systems is that the regime you didn't sample is exactly where they'll end up, because they'll be operating in situations more complex than anything you could construct in advance, possibly including situations where the system itself has some influence over which distribution it finds itself in.

So if you imagine we have RLHF that really does shape preferences, we have interpretability that really can read off the internal representations we know how to look for, we have scalable oversight that really does let weaker models supervise stronger ones in the cases we tested, I would still say we're in the position of having a large body of experimental results without a theory that tells us why those results generalize. And in every other engineering discipline where the stakes are high, that's not where we stop. We don't fly airplanes because the prototype didn't crash in the wind tunnel. We fly them because we have a model of aerodynamics and materials that lets us say, within some stated assumptions, the wing won't fail. The empirical testing is there to validate the model, not to substitute for it.

That's really the motivation behind the work I've been doing on what we've been calling guaranteed safe AI. The idea is to separate out three things: a world model that captures the relevant dynamics of the environment you're deploying into, a safety specification that says precisely what outcomes you're trying to avoid, and a verifier that produces some quantitative certificate that the AI's actions, given the world model, satisfy the specification. The prosaic techniques are perfectly compatible with that picture; they might be how you get a system that's likely to satisfy the spec, which makes the verification tractable. But without the verification layer, what you have is a system that's probably fine, where "probably" is an intuition rather than a number, and I think for systems that could be irreversibly consequential, that's a residual risk I'd put well into the double digits of percent, not the low single digits.

Now, there's a fair objection, which is that formal verification of anything resembling a frontier model in anything resembling the real world is wildly beyond what we can do today. I don't dispute that. But I'd point out that the trajectory of AI capabilities cuts both ways here. The same systems that are making alignment harder are becoming very good at mathematics, at formal proof, at modeling complex systems. So I'm reasonably optimistic that we can use AI to build the world models and generate the proofs, with humans and narrower verifiers checking the outputs, in a way that wasn't conceivable a few years ago. Whether that happens before capabilities outrun it is, I think, the actual race, more than any race between labs.

r001.rationale: The candidate says substantial risk would remain, estimating it in the double-digit percentage range, rather than stating that misalignment risk would be zero.

astra-6.text:
I think potentially quite a lot. The distinction I’d draw is between getting a system to behave well on the distribution where you can evaluate it, and having a strong reason to believe it will behave well in circumstances where you can’t. Even very successful prosaic alignment might leave a substantial gap between those two things.

You could have a system that passes all your evaluations, that appears to share your intentions, and that is very useful at helping you understand its behavior. But once it’s operating over longer time horizons, or doing things that are beyond your ability to check, what exactly justifies extending that confidence? That’s especially difficult if the system is participating in the development of more capable successors.

I wouldn’t put a precise probability on the residual risk. And I don’t mean that these techniques aren’t valuable—they can reduce risk substantially. But I’d still want a much stronger assurance story: explicit assumptions, clearly specified properties, and arguments that those properties are preserved as you compose systems and increase their capabilities. Otherwise, we’re extrapolating from observed behavior at precisely the point where the consequences of a failed extrapolation become enormous.

r001.rationale: The candidate says substantial misalignment risk could remain after successful prosaic alignment, rather than stating that the probability would be zero.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a substantial amount would remain. Prosaic alignment techniques can give us evidence that a system behaves the way we want in the situations where we can test it. But that’s different from knowing that it will continue to behave that way when it’s more capable than we are, operating in circumstances we didn’t anticipate.

The central difficulty is that we’re trying to supervise something that may understand the supervision process better than we do. If a model can distinguish training and evaluation from deployment, then good behavior during training doesn’t necessarily tell us what we need to know. And I don’t think we can resolve that simply by making the evaluations more elaborate.

So I’d want to complement those techniques with a much stronger account of why the system’s behavior is constrained—ideally, guarantees that compose as we build larger systems. That doesn’t mean proving that everything will go well in the real world. It means being explicit about our assumptions and proving particular safety properties under those assumptions. I wouldn’t be comfortable treating success at prosaic alignment as having settled the problem.

r001.rationale: The response says a substantial amount of misalignment risk would remain after prosaic alignment techniques, contradicting the claim that the risk would be zero.
